data.title: Persistent mTORC1 signaling in cell senescence results from defects in amino acid and growth factor sensing
data.authors: Carroll B; Nelson G; Rabanal-Ruiz Y; Kucheryavenko O; Dunhill-Turner NA; Chesterman CC; Zahari Q; Zhang T; Conduit SE; Mitchell CA; Maddocks ODK; Lovat P; von Zglinicki T; Korolchuk VI

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human fibroblasts made senescent by stress, replicative exhaustion or oncogene activation
data.finding: Explains why mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent cells. In human fibroblasts rendered senescent three different ways, mTORC1 is constitutively active and no longer responds to serum or amino acid withdrawal. The defect is upstream, not in mTORC1 itself: it is driven in part by depolarisation of the senescent plasma membrane, which leads to primary cilia defects and a failure to shut off growth-factor signalling, while increased autophagy and high intracellular amino acid levels may act to support the nutrient arm. Correcting these inputs restored sensitivity of the pathway and killed the cells, which frames persistent mTORC1 signalling as a survival dependency of senescent cells rather than a by-product of senescence.
data.abstract_excerpt: Mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and cell senescence are intimately linked to each other and to organismal aging. Inhibition of mTORC1 is the best-known intervention to extend lifespan, and recent evidence suggests that clearance of senescent cells can also improve health and lifespan. Enhanced mTORC1 activity drives characteristic phenotypes of senescence, although the underlying mechanisms responsible for increased activity are not well understood.

extracted_findings.intervention: Senescence induction (oxidative stress, replicative exhaustion, oncogene activation); serum and amino-acid starvation; correction of membrane depolarisation and cilia defects
extracted_findings.target: mTORC1 growth-factor and amino-acid sensing inputs
extracted_findings.effect: Senescent human fibroblasts keep mTORC1 constitutively active and starvation-resistant, and restoring pathway sensitivity killed the cells, suggesting persistent mTORC1 signalling supports senescent-cell survival.
